title: Two-thirds of adults still plan to wear masks in shops and on public transport
meta_description: Limits on social contact and many other coronavirus (COVID-19) restrictions will be eased in England and Scotland from 19 July 2021 and in Wales from 7 August.  What are people looking forward to, and which coronavirus restrictions will they continue to follow?

breadcrumb.text: Two-thirds of adults still plan to wear masks in shops and on public transport

lede: Limits on social contact and many other coronavirus (COVID-19) restrictions will be eased in England and Scotland from 19 July 2021 and in Wales from 7 August. What are people looking forward to, and which coronavirus restrictions will they continue to follow?

body.text: 16 July 2021
Two-thirds (64%) of adults in Great Britain said they still plan to cover their faces in shops, following the lifting of most coronavirus legal restrictions in England from 19 July 2021.
The same percentage (64%) plan to wear masks on public transport, while 60% plan to avoid crowded places.
Over half (54%) of adults said they are looking forward to going on holiday abroad when coronavirus rules end.

In our [latest weekly release from the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/bulletins/coronavirusandthesocialimpactsongreatbritain/16july2021), a large majority of adults continued to feel that wearing face coverings (90%) and social distancing from others not in their household, childcare or support bubble are important (88%) in slowing the spread of COVID-19.

More than half (57%) of adults in Great Britain, surveyed between 7 and 11 July 2021, said they are worried about the plan to remove legal restrictions. This includes one-fifth (20%) who are very worried.

The percentage that believe normal life is a year or more away was 28%, slightly more than the 25% who believed this a year ago, between 8 and 12 July 2020, but down from the peak of 41% who thought so between 16 and 20 September 2020.

The easing of restrictions differs between countries. In England, face coverings will no longer be required by law, but will be required on public transport in London and other parts of the country as a condition of travel.

In Scotland, [restrictions are also being eased on 19 July 2021](https://www.gov.scot/news/level-0-from-19-july/) but there will still be limits on how many people can meet indoors and outdoors, with one-metre physical distancing and a cap of 200 people at weddings and funerals. Face coverings will also continue to be required.

[In Wales, from 17 July 2021](https://gov.wales/next-steps-towards-future-fewer-covid-rules-first-minister) up to six people will be allowed to meet indoors, and indoor events will be permitted for up to 1,000 people seated and up to 200 standing. Most other restrictions in Wales will be lifted from 7 August. However, face coverings will still be required in most indoor public spaces, except for hospitality businesses.

body.text: Mask wearing both in shops and on public transport is likely to be lowest among younger people, with 51% of those aged 16 to 29 years saying they were planning to do so in either setting.

body.text: The percentage of people likely to wear masks in shops increases with age, with 74% of those aged 70 years and over planning to do so. On public transport, 69% of those aged 70 years and over said they plan to wear face coverings compared with 70% aged 50 to 69 years.

body.text: Almost half of adults (49%) plan to maintain social distancing around others they do not live with. The percentage was lowest among those aged 16 to 29 years (31%) and highest among those aged 50 to 69 years (59%).

body.text: Among working adults, 30% plan to work from home. Previous analysis has shown that in 2020, [the proportion of individuals working remotely has been declining since March 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/articles/businessandindividualattitudestowardsthefutureofhomeworkinguk/apriltomay2021) as restrictions began to ease. Evidence from the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey and Business Insights and Conditions Survey suggests individuals and workplaces anticipate increased levels of hybrid working after the pandemic.

body.h2: Younger people are the most likely to want to do activities that involve meeting others
body.h4: Question: Which of these are you looking forward to doing when coronavirus (COVID-19) rules end? Adults in Great Britain, 7 to 11 July 2021.
body.text: People aged 16 to 29 years were the most likely age group to be looking forward to activities that involve meeting others. This age group had the highest percentages wanting to do activities such as meeting indoors with no limits on the number of people (54%), going to the cinema or theatre with no social distancing (47%), staying at someone else’s house with no limits on numbers of guests (46%), or going to concerts or nightclubs (44%).

body.text: Asked how much of a personal risk they thought catching coronavirus was to them, 29% of adults in Great Britain overall considered it to be a very high or high risk and 32% considered it to be a very low or low risk.

body.text: While younger people are more likely than older people to be keen to do things that involve meeting others, those aged 16 to 29 years also considered themselves to have the lowest personal risk from catching coronavirus (COVID-19). 47% of this age group said they considered themselves to be at very low or low risk.

body.text: Even with the plan to ease coronavirus (COVID-19) restrictions in England from 19 July 2021, more adults in Great Britain (28%) still believed that normal life is a year or more away than believed it will return in six months or less (20%), according to those surveyed between 7 and 11 July 2021.

body.h2: More people think it will be at least a year before normal life returns than think it will be within six months
body.h4: Adults in Great Britain, March 2020 to July 2021
body.text: The point at which people thought normal life was the furthest away was between 16 and 20 September 2020, when 41% of people believed it would be at least another 12 months from then.

body.text: This was around the time the [“rule of six” which limited social mixing came into force](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/rule-of-six-comes-into-effect-to-tackle-coronavirus), followed by other restrictions from [limiting the opening hours of certain businesses, such as pubs](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-54242634), to [limits on the number of guests at weddings and civil partnerships](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/pm-commons-statement-on-coronavirus-22-september-2020).

body.h4: Adults in Great Britain, March 2020 to July 2021
body.text: The percentage of adults who believed normal life was at least a year away fell around the start of a second national lockdown in England, in November 2020, which was also when it was revealed that [a COVID-19 vaccine offered significant protection](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-54873105).

body.h2: More people think it will be at least a year before normal life returns than think it will be within six months
body.h4: Adults in Great Britain, March 2020 to July 2021
body.text: In February 2021, it was announced that there was to be a [four-stage roadmap out of lockdown in England](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/pm-statement-to-the-house-of-commons-on-roadmap-for-easing-lockdown-restrictions-in-england-22-february-2021). At around this point, 20% believed that normal life was at least 12 months away, the lowest proportion since the early 2021 lockdown. This then increased over the following months.
